muscles.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) mass of the forearm.
synonyms: extensor radialis longus + extensor radialis brevis (Straus 1941a,b)
extensor carpi radialis (Abdala & Moro 2006; Abdala et al. 2008)
extensor radialis superficialis + extensor carpi intermedius + extensor radialis profundus (Haines 1939; Walker 1973)
extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis (mammals)

consensus.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus and the adjacent supracondylar ridge.
consensus.insertion: Radius, proximal carpals, or (in mammals and some anurans) the metacarpals.
consensus.action: Extends the wrist and abducts (radially deviates) the manus; contributes to elbow extension.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. The proximoventral ridge of the radius, present here and in Pederpes and read by Bishop (2014) in Ossinodus as the extensor carpi radialis insertion. No origin is scored: the ectepicondyle carries the forearm extensors as a group, and Molnar et al. do not divide that group between individual muscles in this taxon — the forearm extensors as a mass are among their highest-confidence reconstructions, the individual muscles within it are not.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. The proximoventral ridge of the radius (Bishop 2014), one of the muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct fairly confidently here. See the brachioradialis row for why the two radial insertions may be one continuous field of scarring.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis
occurrences.insertion: Almost the whole anterolateral surface of the radius, and the lateral surface of the radiale.
occurrences.note: Includes the extensor radialis longus + brevis sensu Straus (1941a,b).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Plesiomorphic tetrapod condition: insertion stops at the radius and proximal carpals.
occurrences.origin: Proximal part of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis
occurrences.note: In Phyllomedusa and other grasping tree frogs the insertion shifts distally onto the metacarpals, convergently with mammals.
occurrences.attachmentNote: In Phyllomedusa and other grasping tree frogs the insertion has shifted distally onto the metacarpals — the same shift mammals made, independently.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis
occurrences.note: Very likely includes the 'extensor metacarpi radialis' and the 'supinator' sensu Meyers (1996).

occurrences.name: Extensor metacarpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. Two heads, both on the processus supracondylaris dorsalis of the humerus — pars ventralis from its ventral surface, pars dorsalis from its dorsal surface, the latter itself two fused bellies separable along their whole length including the tendons. They fuse proximally into one bipennate belly. The common tendon passes through a groove at the distal radius and around the os radiale to insert on the processus extensorius of the carpometacarpus. The radiale is a pulley here, not an attachment, so it gets no row.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis longus + brevis
occurrences.origin: Lateral supracondylar ridge and lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Bases of metacarpals II and III.
occurrences.action: Extends and abducts the hand at the wrist.
occurrences.note: The distal shift of insertion from carpus to metacarpus is a mammalian derived condition.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Distal migration onto the metacarpals, correlated with finer digital control — and convergent with the anuran condition.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the crista supraectepicondylaris, a crest along the proximal border of the ectepicondylus of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal tendon passing under the abductor pollicis longus and under a transverse retinaculum binding it to the distal radius, then splitting into three branches onto the dorsal bases of metacarpals II-IV; the branch to metacarpal III is thickest and that to IV is sometimes absent.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. **The insertion is symmetrical about metacarpal III**, the mid-axis of the metacarpus, and Gambaryan et al. list that symmetry among the primitive monotreme features. They draw a homology conclusion from it: a muscle centred like this is comparable with the REPTILIAN extensor digitorum communis — the humerodorsalis of Haines (1939), already a synonym on `extensor-digitorum` — rather than with the reptilian extensor carpi radialis, which ends more proximally and preaxially. The rows stay on this record; see its homology block.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the proximal and preaxial borders of the ectepicondylus.
occurrences.insertion: As in the long-beaked echidna, but the branch to metacarpal II is considerably thinner and that to metacarpal IV is absent — though Haines (1939) described one.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. A disagreement with Haines over whether the fourth branch exists, kept because the record's own homology note says the interesting variable on this muscle is the level and spread of its insertion rather than its presence.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis
occurrences.origin: Ventral surface of the ectepicondylus parallel to its proximal border, deeper than the extensor digitorum communis.
occurrences.insertion: Three terminal branches onto the dorsal bases of metacarpals II-IV. The tendon passes under the abductor pollicis longus but over that muscle's transverse branch, and there is no transverse retinaculum binding it to the radius as there is in both echidnas.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The full three-branch insertion is retained here where the short-beaked echidna has lost the fourth; the retinaculum that holds the tendon down in Tachyglossidae is absent.

homology.notes: A stable row across all six reptile/amphibian columns plus mammals. The interesting variable is not presence but the proximodistal level of insertion, which shifted distally independently in mammals and in some anurans.
homology.teaching: Ties directly to Abdala & Diogo's finding that distal insertion shifts track fine digital control, and that mammals are not unique in achieving it.

muscles.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
synonyms: extensor carpi ulnaris (Walker 1973; Abdala et al. 2008)

consensus.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
consensus.insertion: Ulna, ulnare, or metacarpal V.
consensus.action: Extends the wrist and adducts (ulnarly deviates) the manus.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. Scored on the posterior ulna with no landmark, deliberately. The posterior ulnar crest is present, and its appearance together with the olecranon is what Molnar et al. read as the separation of this muscle from the triceps at the last common ancestor of Tetrapoda — but in crown tetrapods the crest is identified as the BOUNDARY between the dorsal and ventral forearm musculature rather than as an attachment, so naming it as the insertion would assert more than the source does.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: Ossinodus pueri. Among the muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct 'fairly confidently' here by combining their character mapping with Bishop's (2014) scars, but they do not itemise which scar carries it, so no attachment row is scored.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: Distal part of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Posterolateral face of the ulna, and the ulnare and intermedium.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The postaxial mirror of the extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis, taking the distal part of the same epicondyle where that muscle takes the proximal part.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: = extensor carpi ulnaris + anconeus quartus sensu Holmes (1977).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Extensor carpi ulnaris from the ulnar condyle and proximal ulna, mainly onto the ulnare with a small expansion to the first metacarpal. In Gekko the insertion is restricted to the pisiform — a different carpal, and one of the clearest attachment differences between the two species.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: Confusingly called flexor ulnaris by Meers (2003) despite being a dorsal-mass, radial-innervated muscle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Reported as extensor carpi ulnaris, tendinous from the lateral condyle to the dorsal manus.

occurrences.name: Extensor metacarpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. A stout tendon on the dorsal epicondyle of the humerus, just distal to the common origin of the supinator and the extensor digitorum communis. The belly runs the length of the ulna and its tendon passes around the dorsal condyle of the ulna into the manus, inserting at the proximal end of the major metacarpal on its caudodorsal surface.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus and the posterior border of the ulna.
occurrences.insertion: Base of metacarpal V.
occurrences.action: Extends and adducts the hand at the wrist.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Extensor carpi ulnaris from the laterodistal humeral ectepicondyle and the articular capsule, onto the lateral base of metacarpal V and the craniolateral base of the accessory carpal.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: = extensor carpi ulnaris + anconeus quartus sensu Holmes (1977).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. **Insertion restricted to the pisiform**, where Eublepharis inserts mainly on the ulnare with a small expansion to metacarpal I. A different carpal bone in the two geckos — the sharpest single argument in this dataset against reading one lizard as Lepidosauria.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: Two heads. The humeral head from the apex of the ectepicondylus by an inner-side aponeurosis shared with the extensor digitorum communis and lateralis; the ulnar head from the anterior aspect of the ulna at the level of the proximal end of the radius.
occurrences.insertion: The two heads fuse at the midlength of the antebrachium into a common tendon which passes under a transverse retinaculum at the distal end of the ulna and inserts on digit V by two branches — a proximal one on the postaxial side of its metacarpophalangeal joint and a distal one on the preaxial side of its proximal interphalangeal joint. Distal to the ulnare the tendon is underlaid by a collagen-adipose pad.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. Gambaryan et al. list the extremely distal insertion of this muscle, almost reaching the end of digit V, among the ADVANCED monotreme features — a wrist extensor that has become a digital one.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: Humeral head from the apex of the ectepicondylus, expanding onto its dorsal side, by the inner-side aponeurosis shared with the extensor digitorum communis and lateralis; ulnar head from the anterior aspect of the olecranon up to the level of the proximal end of the radius.
occurrences.insertion: The two heads converge bipennately on a common aponeurosis and the tendon passes under a transverse retinaculum at the end of the ulna to insert extremely distally, on the base of the ungual phalanx of digit V, postaxial to the extensor digitorum lateralis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The most distal of the three: this one reaches the terminal phalanx.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: One head only, the humeral: a fleshy origin on the apex of the ectepicondylus slightly aided by the aponeurosis shared with the extensor digitorum lateralis and communis.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal tendon under the transverse retinaculum at the distal end of the ulna, together with the extensor digitorum lateralis tendon, splitting in the metacarpal region into four branches: three insert in cascade on the postaxial side of the three joints of digit V, and the most proximal thin one deviates postaxially to join the interosseus V lateralis on the outer side of metacarpal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. **The ulnar head is gone** — both echidnas have two heads and the platypus one, so the division is polymorphic within Monotremata and the clade computes as `variable`. A muscle branch ending on another muscle rather than on bone is also worth noting: the fourth branch joins the interosseus.
occurrences.divisionNote: Single against `heads` in both echidnas, on the loss of the caput ulnare.

homology.notes: Constant across Tetrapoda. Meers's (2003) 'flexor ulnaris' for the crocodylian muscle is a naming hazard, not a homology claim — the muscle is an extensor by mass, nerve and action.
homology.teaching: Good demonstration that a muscle's name may contradict its innervation and mass assignment; the nerve wins.

muscles.name: Extensor digitorum
synonyms: extensor digitorum longus (Abdala et al. 2008; Holmes 1977; Dilkes 2000; Meers 2003)

consensus.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal aponeuroses of the digits.
consensus.action: Extends the digits, and secondarily the wrist.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum
occurrences.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal surfaces of the proximal phalanges of digits II, III and IV, by paired tendons.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The most superficial forearm muscle in dorsal view. It serves digits II-IV only — the salamander manus has four digits, digit V having been lost.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Extensor digitorum longus, by tendon from the ulnar condyle onto the proximal ulnar side of metacarpals II-IV. Gekko has four distal tendinous branches inserting on both sides of metacarpals II-IV instead.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Grus americana, from Fisher & Goodman's Origin/Insertion paragraphs. M. extensor digitorum communis: tendinous from the most distal part of the face of the ectepicondylar prominence, with **a wide vinculum passing posteriorly from the distal end of that tendon to insert along a line on the postero-anconal corner of the ulna, just anterior to the row of papillae for the secondary feathers** — a second, aponeurotic attachment tied directly to the flight-feather apparatus. The round tendon runs distad along the antero-anconal ulna, through the tendinal groove at its distal end, onto the fused area of metacarpals III and IV.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. A stout tendon on the dorsal epicondyle of the humerus, in common with the supinator. The tendon runs through a tendinal sulcus at the distal ulna, is bound to the dorsal surface of the alular metacarpal by a retinaculum, then bifurcates: the shorter branch inserts on the caudal surface of the proximal alula, the longer runs in a sulcus of the major metacarpal deep to the extensor longus digiti majoris and inserts on the craniodorsal surface of the proximal end of the first phalanx of the major digit. One row for both branches, because they are two ends of one tendon on one element.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis
occurrences.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus by the common extensor tendon.
occurrences.insertion: Extensor expansions of digits II–V.
occurrences.action: Extends the digits at the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Extensor digitorum communis, from the distal ectepicondylar crest and tendinously near the humeral ectepicondyle, dividing into four principal tendons to the lateral digits. In three of six cases the belly was partly divided in its middle region.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Four distal tendinous branches inserting on **both sides** of metacarpals II-IV, where Eublepharis inserts only on the proximal ulnar side.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis + lateralis
occurrences.divisionNote: Panthera onca. The communis has two bellies, medial and lateral, in all three species. The LATERAL digital extensor is where they part company: one belly here, two in the ocelot and Geoffroy's cat, whose medial belly divides again into two tendons.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera onca. Sanchez et al. describe the bellies and tendons rather than restating the epicondylar origin, which is the standard carnivoran one; the origin row is the lateral epicondyle on that basis and carries no landmark finer than the bone. In the jaguar and the ocelot the extensor digiti I and extensor digiti II arise from the proximal third of the ulnar diaphysis and each divides into two bellies — the digit I belly continuing as two tendons that fuse into an expansion at the distal phalanx, the digit II belly as a single tendon that fuses with the lateral extensor's tendon to the same digit.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis + lateralis
occurrences.divisionNote: Leopardus geoffroyi. FOUR bellies against the jaguar's three, because the lateral digital extensor is clearly divided in two here and its medial belly splits again into two tendons. The ocelot agrees with Geoffroy's cat, not with the jaguar.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leopardus geoffroyi. See the jaguar row; the attachments are the same and the difference is in how many bellies the lateral extensor holds.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the preaxial border of the ectepicondylus, deeper than the extensor carpi ulnaris and sharing its aponeurosis of origin; that aponeurosis also gives rise to the extensor digitorum lateralis.
occurrences.insertion: A flat terminal tendon passing under the retinaculum extensorum, expanding strongly on the dorsum of the manus and splitting into three branches to the ungual phalanges of digits II-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. One of the three specimens carried the pre-mammalian condition as an individual variation: the extensor digitorum communis and the extensor digitorum profundus fused into a single tendon before branching, giving one extensor to all five digits with a humeral and an ulnar head. Gambaryan et al. treat that variant as a model of the ancestral integrity of the digital extensors, and the fibre slip that crosses between the two muscles in Tachyglossus as the other trace of it.

parts.name: Extensor digitorum lateralis
parts.note: Gambaryan et al. give it as Diogo & Abdala's (2010) extensor digiti minimi. Marked disputed because in all three genera its fibres arise from the extensor digitorum communis' own aponeurosis of origin rather than from bone, which is an argument that it is a differentiation of that muscle rather than an independent one. In Zaglossus, two of three specimens also had a fleshy origin directly on the ectepicondylus.

occurrences.divisionNote: The lateralis inserts on digits IV and V — in this genus onto the ungual phalanx of IV and the PREUNGUAL phalanx of V, whose ungual is reduced.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the distal-preaxial angle of the ectepicondylus, deeper than the extensor carpi ulnaris, by two superficial aponeuroses; the outer one is shared with the humeral head of the extensor carpi ulnaris and with the extensor digitorum lateralis, and forms a longitudinal trough housing the belly of the latter.
occurrences.insertion: Three main branches to digits II-IV, the branch to digit II sending a minor sub-branch to the ungual phalanx of digit I and the branch to digit IV a pair of sub-branches to the ungual phalanx of digit V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Some fibres split off the belly to join the extensor digitorum profundus, which is the second trace of the undivided ancestral extensor.
occurrences.divisionNote: The lateralis reaches the ungual phalanges of both digits IV and V here, where in the long-beaked echidna digit V takes only the preungual.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the ectepicondylus, ascending from the crest on its preaxial apex — where it arises under the extensor carpi ulnaris — along the whole proximal border, where it arises over the extensor carpi radialis. Two aponeuroses of origin, the outer shared with the extensor carpi ulnaris and the extensor digitorum lateralis.
occurrences.insertion: On the manus the terminal tendon divides into a superficial sheet splitting to the ungual phalanges of digits I-IV and a deep sheet splitting to those of digits II-IV; the long tendons also send short deep branches to the bases of the preungual phalanges and fuse dorsally with the interdigital tendons of the cutaneus trunci.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The dorsal digital tendons here are continuous with the skin muscle, which is a muscle end no correlate would record — the cutaneus trunci branches run out between the digits and insert on opposing sides of the claws.

parts.name: Extensor digitorum lateralis
parts.note: Rudimentary in this genus: a very thin tendon whose branches to digits IV and V thin out and fuse with the corresponding extensor digitorum communis tendons before insertion.

homology.notes: Universal across limbed tetrapods; one of the least contested rows in Table 1 despite six different names.

muscles.name: Extensores digitorum breves
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass, intrinsic to the manus.
synonyms: extensores digiti brevis (Abdala et al. 2008; Abdala & Moro 2006)
extensores breves superficiales + extensores breves medii (Gaupp 1896)

consensus.origin: Distal radius/ulna, carpals, and metacarpals — dorsal surface.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal aponeuroses of the digits.
consensus.action: Extends the digits; fine positional control independent of the long extensor.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.origin: Carpals at the bases of digits II, III and IV.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal surface of the proximal end of the terminal phalanx of each digit, by long tendons.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Serves digits II-IV, matching the extensor digitorum communis and reflecting the four-digit salamander manus.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: The extensor indicis brevis superficialis arises continuously from the radiale and the short ligament joining radiale and ulnare, lateral to the extensor carpi radialis tendon that attaches to element Y.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the ulnare onto the distalmost phalanx of digits I-V. In Gekko the insertion is on the antepenultimate phalanx except digit I, where it is the first phalanx.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.note: Attachment rows for this taxon describe the foot and have been moved to the pes record.

Rattus norvegicus, the mammal in Abdala & Diogo's Tables 2 and 3. Largely lost or reduced in the therian manus, though a dorsal intrinsic layer persists in some taxa; they note that the reduction of the intrinsic hand musculature is a mammalian trend, not a mammalian elaboration.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Inserts on the **antepenultimate** phalanx of digits II-V and on the first phalanx of digit I, against the distalmost phalanx throughout in Eublepharis. Scored without a side: the dataset has no vocabulary for position along a digit.

homology.notes: A conserved dorsal intrinsic layer of the manus across non-mammalian tetrapods. Its reduction in mammals is part of the broader loss of intrinsic hand muscles that Abdala & Diogo highlight.
homology.teaching: Supporting evidence for the claim that human hands have fewer intrinsic muscles than lizard or salamander hands.

muscles.name: Abductor pollicis longus
synonyms: abductor et extensor digiti I (Brooks 1889; Ribbing 1907; Howell 1936a,b; Straus 1941a,b)
abductor indicis longus (Gaupp 1896; Manzano et al. 2008)

consensus.origin: Dorsal surface of the ulna and/or radius and the interosseous membrane.
consensus.insertion: Base of metacarpal I — or of the most radial metacarpal present.
consensus.action: Abducts and extends the first (most radial) digit; supinates the manus in sprawling taxa.

occurrences.name: Abductor et extensor digiti I
occurrences.origin: Radiale and intermedium.
occurrences.insertion: Distal end of the first metacarpal.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. abductor et extensor digiti I. Wholly intrinsic to the hand — it takes no origin in the forearm, unlike the amniote abductor pollicis longus, which is why the name transfers badly.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.insertion: Digit 2, not digit 1.
occurrences.note: The key case. Adult anurans have lost digit 1, so the most radial digit is digit 2 — and the abductor pollicis longus homologue attaches to it. What determines the attachment is the POSITION of the digit (most radial), not its embryological identity.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.origin: Ulna.
occurrences.insertion: Metacarpal I.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Extensor ossis metacarpi pollicis, the squamate name for this muscle: from the distal border of the ventral surface of the ulna onto the radial border of metacarpal I. Scored on the ulna without a landmark for the distal border, which is not a named process here.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.origin: Posterior surfaces of the ulna, radius and interosseous membrane.
occurrences.insertion: Base of metacarpal I.
occurrences.action: Abducts and extends the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Abductor digiti I longus: from the lateral surface of the ulnar AND radial diaphyses, its tendons held by a dedicated retinaculum in a groove at the craniomedial distal radius, inserting by two tendons at the first digit.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti I longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera onca. A MORE PROXIMAL origin than in Geoffroy's cat, running along the whole lateral edge of the ulna, over the proximal two-thirds of the radius, and onto the interosseous membrane of the forearm. The membrane row matters: a third of this muscle's origin is not on bone at all, so the osteological correlate understates it. No insertion row — Sanchez et al. do not state where it ends in these species.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti I longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leopardus geoffroyi. The same three surfaces as the jaguar and the ocelot but a LESS PROXIMAL origin on the radius — the one difference Sanchez et al. draw for this muscle, and the reason the radius row here carries no `proximal` side where the jaguar's does. Scoring both species is what makes the difference visible; a single Theria row would have had to pick one.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.origin: Adjacent parts of the anterior sides of the radius and ulna, descending from the elbow joint over more than half the length of the radius.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal tendon formed in the distal quarter of the antebrachium, running under its own transverse retinaculum in a groove on the distal end of the radius to the preaxial side of metacarpal I.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The groove on the distal radius is an osteological correlate for the tendon rather than for the muscle.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.origin: The ulna only. More postaxially the anterior surface of the ulna is taken by the extensor digitorum profundus, and the boundary between the two origins is marked on the bone by a rugosity.
occurrences.insertion: Distal aponeuroses on the inner and outer surfaces of the belly fuse into a terminal tendon passing under its own transverse retinaculum at the distal end of the radius to the preaxial side of metacarpal I.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The one genus whose abductor pollicis longus has left the radius entirely, and it leaves a readable boundary: a rugosity on the ulna separating it from the extensor digitorum profundus. Two muscles sharing a bone and marking where one stops.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.origin: Anterior side of the proximal end of the radius and the adjacent part of the ulna.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal tendon under its own transverse retinaculum at the distal end of the radius to the preaxial side of the base of metacarpal I, giving off at the level of the wrist a postaxial branch which passes over the brachioradialis tendon, deeper than every other extensor tendon, to insert on the preaxial side of the ulnare.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The postaxial branch onto the ulnare is unique to this genus, and it is the structure that holds the brachioradialis tendon down in place of the sheath the echidnas use.

homology.notes: Homology of the muscle is secure; what varies is which digit it lands on. Ribbing (1907) argued that Gaupp's (1896) anuran 'abductor pollicis' actually corresponds to the pronator quadratus rather than the abductor pollicis brevis — a caution that the anuran forearm nomenclature is unusually tangled.
homology.teaching: The flagship position-versus-identity example. Pair with the urodele abductor digiti minimi (digit 4) and the counter-case in chickens where digit identity does appear to matter.

muscles.name: Brachioradialis
synonyms: tractor radii (Haines 1939; Walker 1973; Wyneken 2001; Abdala et al. 2008)

consensus.origin: Lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus.
consensus.insertion: Distal radius.
consensus.action: Flexes the elbow; in mammals, brings the forearm to mid-pronation.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. Origin from the convex supinator process on the anterior edge of the humerus, two-thirds of the way along (Coates 1996); the identification of the muscle comes from Eryops, where the supinator process carries the 'supinator longus' (Miner 1925), and from captorhinids, not from this taxon. Insertion on the dorsomesial ridge of the radius, one of the four ridges Bishop (2014) read on the Ossinodus radius and which Molnar et al. report as present here and in Pederpes. Bishop found no break in the scarring between the dorsomesial and proximoventral ridges, so this insertion and the extensor carpi radialis's may not be separate.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. The dorsomesial ridge of the radius, read by Bishop (2014) as the insertion of the brachioradialis ('supinator longus'), with the caution he attaches: there is no break in the muscle scarring between this ridge and the proximoventral ridge, so this insertion and the extensor carpi radialis's may not be separate. Godfrey (1989) made the same kind of reading for the two mesial ridges of the Greererpeton radius, as the boundary between the extensor and flexor masses. Molnar et al. place the separation of the two muscles at Elpistostegalia, marked by a scar or facet distal to the supinator ridge.

occurrences.note: Not an independent muscle in Ambystoma.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.note: = tractor radii sensu Haines (1939), Walker (1973), Wyneken (2001).
Absent in Timon but seemingly present in Sphenodon.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.note: Appears to correspond to the 'supinator' sensu Meers (2003).
Marked '– [but see text]'.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.origin: Proximal two-thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge.
occurrences.insertion: Styloid process of the radius.
occurrences.action: Flexes the elbow, strongest in mid-pronation.
occurrences.note: Anomalous among the radial-innervated group in being an elbow flexor rather than an extensor.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Supinator longus. From the humeral diaphysis immediately caudodistal to the brachialis origin, running up to the cranial surface of the ectepicondylar crest; origin length varied between specimens, in some reaching the proximal diaphysis near the humeral neck. Inserts on the craniomedial distal radius.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera onca. From the proximal third of the CAUDAL surface of the humerus, covering the cranial forearm muscles, to insert medially at the distal end of the radius and on the proximal row of the carpus by a thick flattened tendon. The carpal row is the part worth noting: this record's consensus stops at the distal radius, and in these felids the tendon carries past it. Very well developed in the jaguar and the ocelot, much less so in Geoffroy's cat — the clearest of the size-related differences the paper reports.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.origin: Fleshy from the ventral surface of the ectepicondylus near its proximal border, deeper than the extensor carpi radialis.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal tendon passing under the abductor pollicis longus onto the dorsal projection of the preaxial carpal complex, between its joints with distal carpals II and III; the tendon is held at the distal end of the radius by a connective-tissue sheath.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. **The insertion is not on the radius.** Everywhere else in this dataset the brachioradialis ends on the radius — that is what the name is about — and in all three monotreme genera it passes the radius entirely and ends on the fused radiale + intermedium + centrale, the preaxial carpal complex.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.origin: Fleshy from the ventral surface of the ectepicondylus along its proximal border, only the postaxial part of the origin passing under that of the extensor carpi radialis.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal tendon passing under the abductor pollicis longus onto the dorsal projection of the preaxial carpal complex, between its joints with distal carpals II and III.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Allen (1912) took the radial head of the brachialis for this muscle, which is worth noting because the two do lie together and the mistake is in the older literature the therian rows on this record descend from.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.origin: Fleshy from the ventral surface of the ectepicondylus clear of its proximal border, deeper than both the extensor carpi radialis and the extensor digitorum communis, which has expanded proximally along the ectepicondylar border.
occurrences.insertion: As in the echidnas, onto the preaxial carpal complex; the only real difference is that the tendon is bound to the distal end of the radius by a transverse branch of the abductor pollicis longus tendon rather than by its own sheath.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Same bone, different retaining structure — the tendon is held down by a neighbour's tendon instead of by a ligament of its own.

homology.notes: Present in turtles, crocodylians, Sphenodon and mammals; absent or uncertain in amphibians, most lepidosaurs and birds. Whether this reflects an ancestral muscle with several losses or repeated differentiation from the radial extensor mass is unresolved.

muscles.name: Supinator
synonyms: 'supinator' (Meyers 1996 — avian usage, part of extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis)

consensus.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus, the supinator crest of the ulna, and the radial collateral and annular ligaments.
consensus.insertion: Proximal third of the radius, wrapping around its lateral and anterior surfaces.
consensus.action: Supinates the forearm, independently of elbow position.
consensus.innervation: Radial nerve, deep branch — which pierces the muscle and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. A stout tendon on the dorsal epicondyle of the humerus, shared with the extensor digitorum communis, lying on the cranial surface of the radius deep to the extensor metacarpi radialis. The bulky belly runs nearly half the length of the radius and inserts by semitendinous fibres on its caudodorsal, dorsal and craniodorsal surfaces — the caudodorsal fibres absent in Gavia immer USNM 504983, a difference between two specimens of one species.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.note: Pelecanoides garnoti UMMZ 225241. McKitrick reports the supinator ABSENT in the diving petrel, in the same dissection series that describes it as a bulky belly in the loon; what is left of its field she treats under the ectepicondylo-ulnaris. Her purpose was to test a proposed loon-tubenose sister relationship, which she does not support — so this row is one of the character differences behind that negative result, not a curiosity.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.origin: Lateral epicondyle, supinator crest of the ulna, annular and radial collateral ligaments.
occurrences.insertion: Lateral, posterior and anterior surfaces of the proximal radius.
occurrences.innervation: Deep branch of the radial nerve (C6–C7).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Supinator brevis, from the articular capsule and lateral ligaments of the elbow immediately lateral to the humeral condyle, onto the cranial surface of the proximal two-thirds of the radius. Its origin is capsule and ligament rather than bone.

occurrences.note: Squamates have limited forearm rotation and no unambiguous supinator. Reports of a lepidosaur 'supinator' generally refer to a brachioradialis-like or abductor-pollicis-longus-like muscle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Both supinators: longus from the outer edge of the humerus onto the lower two-thirds of the radius, brevis from the outer condyle along the whole radius. In Gekko the brevis origin is more proximal on the humerus.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.attachmentNote: An insertion surface on the radius.

occurrences.note: Meers (2003) applies the name 'supinator' to what Abdala & Diogo identify as the brachioradialis. This is a naming collision, not a record of the mammalian supinator.
Squamates have limited forearm rotation and no unambiguous supinator. Reports of a lepidosaur 'supinator' generally refer to a brachioradialis-like or abductor-pollicis-longus-like muscle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. The brevis origin sits **more proximally on the humerus** than in Eublepharis.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.origin: Fleshy from the entire ventral surface of the ectepicondylus of the humerus, beneath the other antebrachial extensors, with an aponeurosis of origin on its anterior side running almost to the midlength of the belly.
occurrences.insertion: Fleshy on the preaxial side of the proximal three-quarters of the radius, a little clear of the elbow joint.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The three genera differ in which stretch of the radius is taken: the proximal three-quarters here, the distal two-thirds in Tachyglossus, the proximal half in the platypus.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the ectepicondylus by two aponeuroses covering the anterior and anteromedial sides of the belly, some fibres arising from the proximal quarter of the medial aponeurosis of origin of the extensor digitorum communis.
occurrences.insertion: Fleshy on the anteropreaxial side of the distal two-thirds of the radius, a little clear of the wrist joint.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The only one of the three whose supinator insertion is distal rather than proximal on the radius.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the ectepicondylus, mostly fleshy, aided by an aponeurosis on the anterolateral side.
occurrences.insertion: Fleshy on the anteropreaxial side of the proximal half of the radius, a little clear of the elbow joint.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. This record's homology note calls the therian supinator a muscle with no confidently identified counterpart outside Mammalia; the monotreme rows are the outgroup evidence for that statement rather than against it, since monotremes are mammals.

homology.notes: Included chiefly as a terminology anchor. 'Supinator' is applied by different authors to at least three non-homologous muscles: the crocodylian brachioradialis (Meers 2003), part of the avian extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis (Meyers 1996), and — as 'supinator manus' — the abductor pollicis longus (Haines 1939; Holmes 1977). The therian supinator as a discrete deep antebrachial muscle has no confidently identified counterpart outside Mammalia.
homology.openQuestion: Is the therian supinator a mammalian differentiation from the deep dorsal antebrachial mass, or does it correspond to one of the reptilian muscles that carry the name?
homology.teaching: The worst single name in the comparative forearm literature. Use it to make the point that a name in a table is a pointer to a description, never a homology claim on its own.

muscles.name: Anconeus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass. Often described as a detached distal part of the triceps field.

consensus.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
consensus.insertion: Olecranon and proximal dorsal ulna.
consensus.action: Extends the elbow; stabilises the ulna during pronation/supination.

occurrences.note: Absent in Ambystoma ordinarium, but Haines (1939) reports it in other urodeles such as Salamandra.

occurrences.name: Anconeus
occurrences.note: = epicondylo-cubitalis sensu Gaupp (1896).
Absent in Trachemys but present in Testudo, Pelomedusa, Chelodina and Emys.
Absent in Timon but present in at least some lepidosaurs, including Sphenodon.

occurrences.name: Anconeus
occurrences.note: = anconeus quartus sensu Holmes (1977).

occurrences.name: Anconeus
occurrences.origin: Posterior lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Lateral olecranon and proximal posterior ulna.
occurrences.action: Assists elbow extension; abducts the ulna in pronation.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From the caudal area of the last third of the humerus onto the articular capsule and the lateral surface of the olecranon.

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus lateralis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal surface of the ectepicondylus of the humerus, preaxial to the triceps medialis.
occurrences.insertion: Along the anterior border of the olecranon, descending onto the ulna a little distal to the elbow joint.
occurrences.note: Zaglossus bruijnii. Gambaryan et al. give this as the m. anconeus of Diogo & Abdala (2010) — which is this record — and read it as homologous with the extensor antebrachii ulnaris of lower tetrapods (Haines 1939).

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus lateralis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal surface of the ectepicondylus, preaxial to the triceps medialis.
occurrences.insertion: The anterior border of the olecranon, not descending distal to the elbow joint; the insertion is marked by a rugosity.
occurrences.note: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The shortest insertion of the three, and the only one that leaves a named rugosity.

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus lateralis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal surface of the ectepicondylus, preaxial to the triceps medialis.
occurrences.insertion: Along the anterior border of the olecranon, descending onto the ulna a little distal to the elbow joint.
occurrences.note: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. = m. anconeus sensu Diogo & Abdala (2010). One of the two links in the naming chain that runs the other way: here Gambaryan et al. keep a name of their own for a muscle Diogo & Abdala call by the name this record uses.

homology.notes: Highly variable at the species level within every major clade — present in some turtles and not others, some lepidosaurs and not others, some urodeles and not others. This intraclade variability is itself the finding: the anconeus separates from and refuses to the triceps field readily.
homology.teaching: A caution against reading a single exemplar species as representative of its clade.

muscles.name: Epitrochleoanconeus
synonyms: part of flexor carpi ulnaris (Walker 1973; Abdala et al. 2008)

consensus.origin: Medial epicondyle (entepicondyle) of the humerus.
consensus.insertion: Olecranon / proximal ulna, medially.
consensus.action: Flexes the elbow and stabilises the medial side of the joint; in mammals it forms part of the cubital tunnel roof over the ulnar nerve.

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus (anconeus epitrochlearis)
occurrences.note: Present in many mammals; in humans it is an inconstant muscle replaced by Osborne's ligament over the cubital tunnel. Not the muscle a rat or cat dissection guide calls the epitrochlearis. Campbell's rat guide describes that one as a thin medial sheet of the upper arm that EXTENDS the forearm — a latissimus-associated muscle reaching the olecranon — whereas the epitrochleoanconeus runs from the medial epicondyle to the olecranon over the ulnar nerve. The names differ by two letters and the muscles are not the same; no source held here establishes what the lab epitrochlearis is homologous to, so it has no record.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From the humerus distal to the caudal opening of the entepicondylar foramen, onto the medial and caudal surfaces of the olecranon, sharing fibres distally with the ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris. The entepicondylar foramen is a carnivoran feature and locates this origin precisely.

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus medialis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal surface of the entepicondylus of the humerus, close to its tip.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior projection of the olecranon apex.
occurrences.note: Zaglossus bruijnii. = m. epitrochleoanconeus sensu Diogo & Abdala (2010), and homologous with the flexor antebrachii ulnaris of lower tetrapods (Jouffroy et al. 1971). It is separated from the triceps medialis by the nerves converging on the entepicondylar foramen, which is how the two are told apart.

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus medialis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal surface of the entepicondylus, close to its tip.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior projection of the olecranon apex.
occurrences.note: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Identical in all three genera, which is worth recording as sameness rather than omitting: three species examined, one arrangement found.

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus medialis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal surface of the tip of the entepicondylus.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior projection of the olecranon apex.
occurrences.note: Ornithorhynchus anatinus.

homology.notes: Present in all six non-mammalian columns of Table 1. Note the contrast with the anconeus: similar name, opposite mass (ventral vs dorsal) and opposite nerve (ulnar vs radial).
homology.teaching: Pair the anconeus and epitrochleoanconeus explicitly. Near-identical names, opposite sides of the elbow, opposite nerves. A good exam question.

muscles.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
synonyms: part of flexor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris (Diogo & Abdala 2007; Diogo 2007)

consensus.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus and the proximal ulna.
consensus.insertion: Ulnare/pisiform and metacarpal V.
consensus.action: Flexes and adducts (ulnarly deviates) the wrist.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: Part of the flexor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris sensu Diogo & Abdala (2007).
occurrences.origin: Distal portion of the medial epicondyle of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Much of the posterior edge of the ulna, with a slip to the lateral faces of the ulnare and intermedium.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Described as the mirror image of the flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis. The four muscles taking the two epicondyles — two flexors medially, two extensors laterally, each pair split proximal and distal — are the clearest instance of the dorsal/ventral mirroring the paper reports for the antebrachium.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: Dilkes (2000): present in all major extant reptile groups.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the ulnar condyle of the humerus and the entire laterodorsal border of the ulna onto the pisiform.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tendinous at the distomedial humerus, fleshy at the ventral carpus.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: Medial epicondyle (humeral head) and olecranon/posterior ulna (ulnar head).
occurrences.insertion: Pisiform, hamate and base of metacarpal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Two heads: caput ulnare from the caudal and medial olecranon, caput humerale from the distal humeral entepicondyle. The ulnar head inserts on the lateral surface of the accessory carpal (pisiform) and the wrist fascia, its ligament continuing to the base of metacarpal V.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: Dilkes (2000): present in all major extant reptile groups.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: Caput humerale from the apex and postaxial part of the distal border of the entepicondylus, with an inner-side aponeurosis shared with the caput humerale superficiale of the flexor digitorum profundus; caput ulnare from the posterior-postaxial side of the ulna along almost its whole length, excluding the distal end but including the olecranon.
occurrences.insertion: The two heads form a common aponeurosis and a flat tendon running to the proximal apex of the pisiform, from which three pisometacarpal ligaments descend to the bases of metacarpals II-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The pisiform is used as a lever exactly as the prepollex is on the other side of the wrist: it lengthens the moment arm for flexion and lateral abduction, and the ligaments carry the pull on to the carpometacarpal II-IV joints.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: Caput humerale from the dorsal side of the postaxial distal angle of the entepicondylus, itself divided into two portions of which the posterior fuses with the caput ulnare; caput ulnare from the posterior-postaxial side of the ulna throughout its length.
occurrences.insertion: Both heads onto the pisiform, from which pisometacarpal ligaments descend to metacarpals II-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The humeral head is itself split here, its anterior portion staying separate from the ulnar head and its posterior portion fusing with it — a division within a division that neither of the other two genera shows.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: Caput humerale from the apex and postaxial part of the distal border of the entepicondylus, unipennate; caput ulnare tripennate, from the posterior-postaxial surface of the olecranon, descending a little distal to the elbow joint.
occurrences.insertion: A short thick common tendon on the proximal apex of the pisiform. Ligaments from the pisiform to the metacarpals are ABSENT.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The pisometacarpal ligaments both echidnas use to relay the pull onward are missing, which is the same difference the flexor carpi radialis shows on the preaxial side: in the platypus both wrist flexors act on the wrist alone.

homology.notes: Universal. Ulnar innervation is constant and is the criterion that separates it from the extensor carpi ulnaris despite similar names and adjacent positions.

muscles.name: Flexor carpi radialis
synonyms: pronator superficialis (Sullivan 1962; Shellswell & Wolpert 1977; Meyers 1996; Dilkes 2000)

consensus.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus.
consensus.insertion: Bases of metacarpals II and III, or the distal radius/carpals in plesiomorphic taxa.
consensus.action: Flexes and abducts (radially deviates) the wrist.

occurrences.name: Flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. An area of scarring on the face of the radius between the ventral radial crest and the ventral median ridge, read by Bishop (2014) as the insertion — the prominent crest itself carries no scarring. Scored as radius/ventral with no landmark, because the attachment is the surface between two named ridges rather than either of them. Molnar et al. place the separation of this muscle from the humeroantebrachialis at the last common ancestor of crown tetrapods, marked by the appearance of the ventral median ridge.

occurrences.name: Flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis
occurrences.origin: Proximal portion of the medial epicondyle of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Anterior face of the radius, with a slip crossing the wrist to the radiale.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Obscured along most of its length by the flexor digitorum communis. Preaxial member of the pair that divides the medial epicondyle between them.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.note: In turtles the pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis are usually distinct muscles, though Holmes designated the pronator teres a 'head of the flexor carpi radialis'.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the inner condyle of the humerus, tendinously onto the radiale and muscularly onto the distal radius.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.note: Seems to correspond to the pronator superficialis sensu Sullivan (1962), Shellswell & Wolpert (1977), Meyers (1996) and Dilkes (2000).

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.origin: Medial epicondyle by the common flexor tendon.
occurrences.insertion: Bases of metacarpals II and III.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From the middle region of the medial end of the humeral entepicondyle, held by its own retinaculum at the radial carpal, inserting by two loose tendons onto the proximal palmar regions of metacarpals II and III.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.origin: Along the ventral side of the entire distal border of the entepicondylus from its apex to the humeral condyle, interrupted by the origin of the caput humerale profundum of the flexor digitorum profundus; aponeuroses of origin on the inner side shared with the pronator teres and on the outer side with the caput humerale superficiale.
occurrences.insertion: A wide flat tendon to the proximal apex of the prepollex, which articulates with the preaxial carpal complex; from the prepollex the pull is relayed by ligaments to the distal carpals and metacarpals I-III.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. **The insertion is on the prepollex**, in all three genera — the element `GAPS.md` §1 singles out as the anuran position-versus-identity case. Monotremes did not lose digit I and have one anyway, and hang more on it than anurans do. The distal ligaments here make it a lever for the carpometacarpal I-III joints as well as for the wrist.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.origin: As in the long-beaked echidna but uninterrupted by the caput humerale profundum, with relatively shorter fibres and more developed aponeuroses of origin, which descend about half the length of the antebrachium.
occurrences.insertion: A flat tendon to the proximal apex of the prepollex, which is connected to the preaxial carpal complex and, by two ligaments, to distal carpals I and II.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Two ligaments to the distal carpals rather than the long-beaked echidna's relay to metacarpals I-III.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.origin: As in Tachyglossidae, but the belly is flattened in the parasagittal plane and more sharply bipennate: the anterior penna bears an aponeurosis facing the humeral condyle and the radius, the posterior penna two, shared with the pronator teres and the caput humerale superficiale.
occurrences.insertion: A round tendon on the proximal apex of the prepollex, with no ligamentous relay onward.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The prepollex insertion is shared with both echidnas; what is missing here is the onward ligamentous transfer to the carpals and metacarpals, so the muscle acts on the wrist alone.

homology.notes: Constant across Tetrapoda. The boundary with the pronator teres is fluid — Holmes (1977) and Dilkes (2000) treat them as one muscle in several taxa, Abdala & Diogo separate them.

muscles.name: Pronator teres
synonyms: part of flexor carpi radialis (Holmes 1977; Dilkes 2000)
pronator profundus (Sullivan 1962; Shellswell & Wolpert 1977; Meyers 1996; Dilkes 2000)

consensus.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (and the coronoid process of the ulna in mammals).
consensus.insertion: Lateral surface of the radial shaft.
consensus.action: Pronates the forearm; assists elbow flexion.

occurrences.note: Not differentiated in Ambystoma; the urodele forearm lacks a discrete pronator teres.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.note: Ribbing (1907) and Gaupp (1896) disagreed about which anuran muscle this is — flexor antebrachii lateralis superficialis + profundus, or flexor antebrachii medialis.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tendinous at the ventrodistal humerus, fleshy on the ventral carpus. Note the carpal rather than radial insertion — Klinkhamer et al. report it that way for Crocodylus.

occurrences.name: Pronator superficialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. A stout tendon from the tuberculum supracondylare ventrale of the humerus, slightly proximal and partly superficial to the origin of the pronator profundus, inserting by tendinous fibres along the cranioventral surface of the proximal third of the radius. No landmark is asserted for the humeral origin: McKitrick flags 'homology problems with Baumel et al.' over whether the tuberculum supracondylare ventrale and the ventral epicondyle are the same thing, and naming the entepicondyle here would settle by fiat what she leaves open. The tendon of origin fans into an aponeurosis continuous with the humerocarpal band.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.origin: Medial epicondyle (humeral head) and coronoid process of the ulna (ulnar head).
occurrences.insertion: Middle of the lateral radial shaft.
occurrences.note: The median nerve passes between the two heads — a common entrapment site.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From the medioproximal and cranial region of the humeral entepicondyle in two bellies, onto the cranial surface of the mediodistal radius.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.origin: A round area on the ventral side of the entepicondylus, plus an aponeurosis on the posterior side of the muscle shared with the flexor carpi radialis.
occurrences.insertion: Preaxial side of the radius distal to its midlength.
occurrences.note: Zaglossus bruijnii. The most superficial muscle on the inner surface of the antebrachium in all three genera.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.origin: A narrower area on the ventral side of the entepicondylus than in the long-beaked echidna, with aponeuroses of origin on both the posterior side — shared with the flexor carpi radialis — and the anterior side of the belly.
occurrences.insertion: Preaxial side of the distal part of the radius.
occurrences.note: Tachyglossus aculeatus.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the apex of the entepicondylus.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal aponeuroses on the anterior and posterior sides of the belly fuse into a flat tendon inserting on the POSTERIOR side of the radius close to its midlength.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Both echidnas insert on the preaxial side of the radius and the platypus on its posterior side, which for a pronator is a change in the line of action and not just in position.

homology.notes: Present in every column except Caudata. Its absence in urodeles is consistent with the limited forearm rotation of a sprawling, aquatic-ancestral limb; pronation capability increases with the differentiation of this muscle.
homology.teaching: Useful for linking muscle differentiation to a functional capability — forearm rotation — that appears above the urodele node.

muscles.name: Pronator quadratus
synonyms: pronator profundus (Ribbing 1907; Straus 1942; Walthall & Ashley-Ross 2006; Moro & Abdala 2004; Abdala et al. 2008)

consensus.origin: Distal ventral (anterior) surface of the ulna.
consensus.insertion: Distal ventral surface of the radius.
consensus.action: Pronates the forearm; binds the distal radioulnar joint.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.origin: Medial side of the ulna, the ulnare and the intermedium.
occurrences.insertion: Radiale and the base of the first metacarpal.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. pronator profundus. It crosses from the postaxial to the preaxial side of the wrist, which is what makes it a pronator rather than a flexor.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.note: Ribbing (1907) held that Gaupp's (1896) anuran 'abductor pollicis' is in fact the pronator quadratus, not the abductor pollicis brevis.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.note: Probably corresponds to part of Walker's (1973) pronator profundus; the remainder is the pronator accessorius.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.attachmentNote: A discrete origin fossa on the ulna — the same proximal-ulnar origin Klinkhamer et al. report for Crocodylus.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy at the proximomedial ulna to the posterodistal radius.

occurrences.name: Pronator profundus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. A unipennate muscle from a stout tendon on the tuberculum supracondylare ventrale, distal and partly deep to the pronator superficialis and proximal and partly deep to the flexor digitorum superficialis, running the whole length of the radius and inserting by fleshy and semitendinous fibres along its ventral surface. The two pronators share one humeral field and are separated by depth and by the level of their tendons, not by different bones — which is why both rows read the same and the difference is in this note.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.origin: Distal quarter of the anterior ulna.
occurrences.insertion: Distal quarter of the anterior radius.
occurrences.action: Pronates the forearm; the prime mover for unresisted pronation.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. The deepest muscle of the distal medial forearm: from the medial surface of the distal ulna onto the craniomedial and medial radius, its insertion continuous distally with the palmar radiocarpal and ulnocarpal ligaments.

homology.notes: Present in all six non-mammalian columns and in mammals — unlike the pronator teres, which urodeles lack. The deep pronator is therefore the plesiomorphic member of the pronator group.

consensus.origin: Distal ulna, deep to the pronator quadratus.
consensus.insertion: Distal radius and adjacent carpals.
consensus.action: Assists pronation.

homology.notes: Present only in turtles and lepidosaurs on this sampling. Walker (1973) treated it and the pronator quadratus together as a single 'pronator profundus', so the split is Abdala & Diogo's interpretation rather than a universally accepted division.

muscles.name: Flexor digitorum longus / communis
synonyms: flexor digitorum communis longus (Manzano 1996; Manzano et al. 2008b)
flexor primordialis communis + flexor accessorius communis (Ribbing 1907)

consensus.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus, with additional heads from the radius and ulna.
consensus.insertion: Palmar surfaces of the phalanges, via a common tendon plate that divides into digital tendons.
consensus.action: Flexes the digits and the wrist; the principal grasping muscle.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum communis
occurrences.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Palmar aponeurosis, continuing as four tendons to the proximal end of the distal phalanx of each digit.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Walthall & Ashley-Ross use flexor digitorum communis; Francis (1934) called the same muscle flexor primordialis communis, the name used for its hindlimb counterpart here. The aponeurosis, not the bone, is the functional insertion — the tendons are its continuation.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: = flexor primordialis communis + flexor accessorius communis sensu Ribbing (1907).

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: Probably also includes the 'pronator radii teres' sensu McMurrich (1903a) and Holmes (1977), at least in Sphenodon and lizards.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the medial part of the ulnar condyle and the distal two-thirds of the ulna, onto the terminal phalanges of digits I and II.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tendinous at both ends; reaches digit 2 of the manus.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Grus americana, from Fisher & Goodman's Origin/Insertion paragraphs. M. flexor digitorum profundus: fleshy from the postero-palmar surface of the ulna, from the distal extent of the distal superficial joint ligament out to about one-third of the ulna. Its tendon crosses the wrist beneath the superficial sheath and **hooks around the anterior aspect of the pisiform process of the metacarpus** — the avian carpometacarpus is fused, so the insertion is scored on the metacarpal series with the pisiform process named as the pulley.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum superficialis + flexor digitorum profundus
occurrences.origin: Medial epicondyle, coronoid process, radius (superficialis); anteromedial ulna and interosseous membrane (profundus).
occurrences.insertion: Middle phalanges (superficialis) and distal phalanges (profundus) of digits II–V.
occurrences.innervation: Median nerve; the ulnar half of the profundus by the ulnar nerve.
occurrences.note: The mammalian split into superficial and deep layers with staggered phalangeal insertions is a derived elaboration of a single ancestral flexor plate.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Flexor digitorum profundus, five heads: three humeral (caput humerale laterale, mediale and profundus), one ulnar and one with radial and ulnar origins. The superficialis is not independent — it arises from the surface of the profundus itself and sends three thin tendons to digits II-IV, which is why this record's Theria occurrence lists both.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: Probably also includes the 'pronator radii teres' sensu McMurrich (1903a) and Holmes (1977), at least in Sphenodon and lizards.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum superficialis + profundus
occurrences.divisionNote: Panthera onca. Seven heads across the two muscles: the superficialis unites an ulnar and a radial head into one belly, which in the jaguar is thick and flattened and divides into four tendons, one per finger; the profundus has five, of which three arise from the humerus completely separately and in one median plane. The SECOND head alone forms the tendon of digit I and the remaining four serve digits II to V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera onca. The radial or deep head of the profundus arises from the distal middle third of the radius and ulna, which is the radius/distal row; the humeral heads take the medial epicondyle. Each tendon runs under the proximal annular ligament, and those of digits II to V continue under the distal annular ligament to insert on the PALMAR side of the distal phalanx. In the jaguar this belly carries TWO SESAMOID BONES — a species-level observation with a skeletal element behind it, and the only one in this paper that a dry specimen could confirm.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum profundus
occurrences.origin: Four heads. Caput humerale superficiale from the ventral side of the distal border of the entepicondylus throughout its length; caput humerale profundum compactly from the ventral side of the spina entepicondyli; caput olecrani and caput ulnare undifferentiated from one another and arising together from the proximal three-quarters of the posterior side of the ulna including the olecranon.
occurrences.insertion: The heads converge on a common tendon which splits, at a palmar sesamoid, into branches to the ventral bases of the ungual phalanges of digits I-V, II-V or II-IV depending on the specimen.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. = m. flexor digitorum longus sensu Diogo & Abdala (2010), which is this record. The variable digital formula is the reduction of the marginal fingers this genus is going through, and it is why the authors recommend Z. bartoni — which keeps all five claws — as the better model. In one specimen a few deep fibres arose from the distal quarter of the posterior radius, which they read as a rudiment of the therian caput radiale.

parts.name: Caput humerale profundum
parts.note: Identified by Gambaryan et al. as the retained ulnocarpalis; see the contrahentium-caput-longum record.

parts.name: Caput radiale
parts.note: A few deep fibres from the posterior radius in one specimen only, read as a rudiment of the therian head.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum profundus
occurrences.origin: As in the long-beaked echidna; the origin of the united caput ulnare et olecrani is outlined on the ulna by two crests.
occurrences.insertion: A large palmar sesamoid is embedded in the common tendon at the point of branching, so that the common tendon inserts on the proximal apex of that bone and five digital branches leave its distal end for the ungual phalanges; the proximal paw pad attaches to its ventral side.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The sesamoid is large enough here that the muscle does not reach the digits directly at all — it ends on a bone in its own tendon, and a second set of tendons continues from that bone. Five digits, against a variable II-V or II-IV in the long-beaked echidna.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum profundus
occurrences.origin: Caput humerale superficiale from the distal border of the entepicondylus — the biggest and, with fibres only about 2 mm long, by far the strongest head; caput humerale profundum with long fibres from the ventral side of the spina entepicondyli; caput olecrani and the smaller caput ulnare from the posterior side of the ulna below the midlength of the bone, here fully separate from one another.
occurrences.insertion: Two palmar sesamoids on the thick common tendon at the level of the carpus. The medial one gives the terminal tendons of digits I-III and the lateral one those of digits IV and V; all five insert on the bases of the ungual phalanges. The thin tendon of the caput humerale profundum inserts on the two sesamoids separately, deeper than the common tendon. Four thick elastin bands run from the sesamoids between the digits into the swimming membrane beyond the claws.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Gambaryan et al. call this muscle a combination of extreme specialisation and profound primitiveness. The specialisation is the caput humerale superficiale: 2 mm fibres give enormous force for underwater rowing and cost the animal finger extension, which is why it knuckle-walks. The primitiveness is the caput humerale profundum, scored on `contrahentium-caput-longum`.

homology.notes: The long digital flexor is universal. What varies is the degree of subdivision — a single plate in amphibians and reptiles, two layers with different insertion levels in mammals.
homology.teaching: Good for showing that a mammalian 'novelty' (superficialis/profundus) is a subdivision of something already present, not a new muscle.

consensus.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus.
consensus.insertion: Palmar aponeurosis.
consensus.action: Tenses the palmar aponeurosis; weak wrist flexion.

occurrences.note: Marked '– [but see text]'.
Absent in Timon, but some lepidosaurs do have a comparable structure.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.note: Absent in roughly 15% of humans unilaterally or bilaterally, and absent in many other mammals.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From the caudomedial margin of the distal humeral entepicondyle onto the palmar fascia, connected indirectly to the radial sesamoid and the accessory carpal. Its insertion is aponeurotic throughout, so it leaves no distal correlate.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.divisionNote: Panthera onca. FIVE tendons, as in the ocelot and against four in Geoffroy's cat. A division count that differs between three species of one family, which is the kind of difference a clade-level row cannot hold at all.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera onca. The palmaris longus lies medial in the forearm and ends by attaching to the tendons of the flexor digitorum superficialis at the proximal end of the middle phalanx — so its insertion is on another muscle's tendons, not on bone, and the phalangeal row is where those tendons land.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.divisionNote: Leopardus pardalis. Five tendons, as in the jaguar.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leopardus pardalis. The palmaris longus lies medial in the forearm and ends by attaching to the tendons of the flexor digitorum superficialis at the proximal end of the middle phalanx — so its insertion is on another muscle's tendons, not on bone, and the phalangeal row is where those tendons land.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.divisionNote: Leopardus geoffroyi. FOUR tendons, against five in both the jaguar and the ocelot. Sanchez et al. do not say which digit goes unserved; the parts here are named on the assumption it is the first, which is the usual pattern of loss in the carnivoran manus and is flagged rather than asserted.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leopardus geoffroyi. The palmaris longus lies medial in the forearm and ends by attaching to the tendons of the flexor digitorum superficialis at the proximal end of the middle phalanx — so its insertion is on another muscle's tendons, not on bone, and the phalangeal row is where those tendons land.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.note: Zaglossus bruijnii. Absent, and Gambaryan et al. list the absence among the primitive features of monotremes as a whole. What stands in its place is a bundle of the cutaneus trunci running down the flexor side of the antebrachium to the wrist and joining, through the fascia palmaris manus, the preaxial side of the common tendon of the flexor digitorum profundus near its branching point — which they call the apparent predecessor of the therian palmaris longus. A skin muscle occupying the position of a limb muscle that does not yet exist.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.note: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Absent, and without even the cutaneus trunci bundle the long-beaked echidna has in its place.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.note: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Absent. Here the cutaneus trunci runs to the EXTENSOR side of the antebrachium instead, terminating at the wrist in a subcutaneous aponeurosis that splits into four interdigital branches, each bifurcating to insert on opposing sides of the claws of adjacent digits.

homology.notes: Quoted deliberately. Abdala & Diogo list this as one of the two structures (with the 'rhomboideus') whose homology with the mammalian muscle of the same name is explicitly under-supported. Their stated requirement: a detailed analysis of the innervation and development of the 'rhomboideus' and 'palmaris longus' across a broader sample of amphibian and reptilian taxa.
homology.openQuestion: Is the turtle 'palmaris longus' homologous with the mammalian palmaris longus, or an independently differentiated superficial flexor?
homology.teaching: An honest example of a named, textbook-familiar muscle whose deep homology is not actually established.

consensus.origin: Distal ulna.
consensus.insertion: Carpus, giving rise to the contrahentes digitorum.
consensus.action: Flexes and adducts the digits toward the axis of the hand.

occurrences.name: Contrahentium caput longum
occurrences.origin: Internal surface of the ulna and the fascia connecting radius and ulna.
occurrences.insertion: An extensive tendon connecting the carpal bones.
